title: Greek Fire
description: The Byzantine sea weapon, the siphon that threw it, and a recipe that was never written down

concepts.title: Fire on the Water
concepts.contentHtml:
In 941 a large Rus fleet led by Prince Igor of Kiev crossed the Black Sea toward Constantinople, while the main Byzantine navy was away fighting Arab fleets in the Mediterranean. Emperor Romanos I had about fifteen old ships patched up in the city's harbors, fitted with fire-throwing tubes and sent out under the official Theophanes. The Italian diplomat Liudprand of Cremona, writing some two decades later, says the Rus surrounded the little squadron expecting an easy capture and were met with jets of fire. Many leapt into the sea rather than burn. The invasion collapsed.

The name you've probably heard, Greek fire, is a later Western name, common from the Crusades onward, and Western writers applied it to almost any incendiary. The Byzantines, who called themselves Romans, named the weapon "sea fire," "liquid fire" or "manufactured fire."

The usual origin story comes from the chronicler Theophanes the Confessor, writing in the early 9th century. He says that around 672 a refugee architect named Kallinikos came from Heliopolis in Syria (Baalbek, in modern Lebanon) and devised a sea fire that burned the Arab ships attacking the city "with all hands." Two cautions apply. Theophanes also mentions fire-carrying ships shortly before Kallinikos arrives, so Kallinikos may have improved an existing weapon rather than invented one. And the siege itself is disputed. Its traditional dates, 674 to 678, rest heavily on Theophanes, and the historian Marek Jankowiak has argued that the main Arab attack came earlier, in 667 to 669.1 Fire ships helped again against the great Arab siege of 717 to 718.

concepts.title: The Siphon
concepts.contentHtml:
Having the fuel wasn't enough; delivering it took a second device. Byzantine texts describe a siphon, a bronze tube mounted at a warship's prow, through which the burning liquid was projected at enemy ships. Around 900 the military manual of Emperor Leo VI, the Tactica, mentions bow siphons, small hand-held siphons that Leo claimed to have invented, and pots of fire thrown by hand. In 941 the defenders reportedly mounted siphons amidships and at the stern as well as at the bow. Writing in the 1140s, the princess and historian Anna Komnene described a fleet of 1099 whose prows carried gilded bronze and iron lion heads that seemed to spit the fire from their mouths.

No surviving text explains the machinery. In 1977 John Haldon and Maurice Byrne proposed a design with a bronze tank of fuel preheated over a brazier, a pump to pressurize it, and a swiveling nozzle. In 2002 Haldon guided a team that built a working version for a television documentary. Modern welding couldn't make a heated tank safe under pressure, so they moved the pump between tank and nozzle. The device threw a jet of burning petroleum-based fuel at over 1,000 °C to a range of about 15 meters, and the jet curved downward, which suited attacks on low-lying galleys.

The sources also describe how the weapon behaved. It burned on water and was hard to put out; sand, strong vinegar or old urine were said to work. Arab crews learned to keep out of range and to hang felt or hides soaked in vinegar over their ships. With a range of meters rather than hundreds of meters, it was a weapon for close fighting.

concepts.title: A Secret Kept Too Well
concepts.contentHtml:
Around 950 Emperor Constantine VII wrote a handbook of statecraft for his son Romanos, now called De Administrando Imperio. In it he says the liquid fire was revealed by an angel to Constantine the Great, the first Christian emperor, who ordered that it be made only for Christians and only in the imperial city, and never handed to foreigners. He adds a cautionary tale about an official bribed to give some to an enemy, who was struck down by flame from heaven as he entered a church. The 11th-century chronicler George Kedrenos claimed that a family descended from Kallinikos kept the secret into his own day, though modern scholars find that unlikely.

Knowledge was probably split among different people, so that crews knew only how to work the siphon. The most widely accepted view is that the fuel was petroleum-based. Crude oil seeps naturally around the Black Sea and the Caucasus, and the same handbook lists oil sources there; resins may have thickened it. Older theories don't hold up. Saltpeter, the main ingredient of gunpowder, doesn't appear in Mediterranean warfare before the 13th century, and quicklime ignites only with water, while this fire was poured onto decks and thrown in pots.

The weapon fades from the record after the 12th century, and no source confirms its use against the crusaders who attacked Constantinople in 1203 and 1204. Suggested reasons include a run-down navy, lost access to oil regions as the empire shrank, or the death of the few who knew the process. Muslim armies had their own naphtha incendiaries, used by specialist troops called naffatun. The exact recipe and siphon design remain unknown, though a petroleum flamethrower of this kind has been shown to work.

title: Roman Concrete
description: Volcanic ash, seawater chemistry and the hot-mixing method behind Roman structures that still stand

concepts.title: A Harbor Poured into the Sea
concepts.contentHtml:
Between about 22 and 15 BCE, Herod the Great built an artificial harbor at Caesarea Maritima on the coast of Judea, where there was no natural shelter. Its breakwaters were made partly of concrete laid in the open sea, and the key ingredient came by ship from Italy: volcanic ash from the Bay of Naples, around Puteoli, today's Pozzuoli. The Romans called it pulvis puteolanus, "Puteoli dust," the origin of the modern word pozzolana.

The architect Vitruvius, writing around 25 BCE, explained why it was worth shipping. A powder found around Baiae and the towns near Mount Vesuvius, he wrote, when mixed with lime and rubble, set hard even in piers built in the sea. For underwater work he recommended two parts of this ash to one of lime, packed into wooden forms set in the water. In the 1st century CE Pliny the Elder added that this dust, once submerged, became "a single stone mass, impregnable to the waves and every day stronger."

That last phrase sounds like boasting. Modern concrete made with Portland cement is expected to deteriorate in seawater within decades, especially once salt reaches its steel reinforcement and rusts it. Yet Roman harbor concrete at Caesarea, Baiae, the port of Cosa and elsewhere survives in the sea after two thousand years. Explaining why took modern mineralogy, and the answer turned out to be partly what Pliny said.

concepts.title: Minerals That Grow in Seawater
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2017 the geologist Marie Jackson and colleagues published analyses of Roman harbor concrete in the journal American Mineralogist. They found that seawater percolating through the concrete had slowly dissolved parts of the volcanic ash and grown new minerals in its pores and cracks: phillipsite, a zeolite, and aluminous tobermorite, a rare platy crystal that is usually made in the laboratory only with heat. These interlocking crystals appear to have reinforced the material over time, so the sea helped finish the concrete.

The same chemistry, a reaction between lime and volcanic ash called the pozzolanic reaction, underlies Roman building on land. The Pantheon in Rome, completed under Hadrian and probably dedicated around 126 CE, has a concrete dome 43.3 meters across that remains the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world. Its builders graded the aggregate, using heavier stone low down and lighter volcanic tuff and pumice toward the top, and thinned the shell toward the open oculus, 9 meters wide.

Careful comparison matters here. Roman concrete is not simply better than modern concrete. Portland cement concrete is generally stronger in compression, gains strength in days rather than slowly over years, and can be reinforced with steel to carry tension, which Roman concrete never was. The Roman advantage is chemical durability in particular settings, above all seawater, and the absence of steel to rust. Engineers now study Roman mixes not to copy them wholesale but to borrow ideas for longer-lasting and lower-carbon cements.

concepts.title: Hot Mixing and Self-Healing Cracks
concepts.contentHtml:
Roman concrete is dotted with small white lumps of lime, a few millimeters across. Archaeologists long read these lime clasts as a sign of careless mixing. In January 2023 a team led by Admir Masic of MIT, with first author Linda Seymour, argued in Science Advances that they were a feature. Studying concrete from Privernum, a Roman site in central Italy, they concluded that builders had used quicklime (burned limestone) directly in the mix, instead of, or alongside, lime first slaked with water into a paste. The reaction gives off heat, and this hot mixing leaves brittle, reactive lime clasts.

When a crack runs through the concrete it tends to pass through these clasts. Water seeping in dissolves calcium from them, which recrystallizes as calcium carbonate and seals the crack. The team made hot-mixed samples, cracked them on purpose and ran water through: within two weeks the cracks had sealed and the flow stopped, while control samples made without quicklime kept leaking. In December 2025 a team including Masic reported in Nature Communications on an unfinished building site at Pompeii, abandoned at the eruption of 79 CE, where quicklime had been premixed with dry volcanic ash before water was added: direct archaeological support for hot mixing.

Roman concrete was partly lost. Lime mortar never vanished, but after the western empire's building economy collapsed, the ash supply chains, the organized workforce and the habit of casting huge vaults faded. For the Eddystone Lighthouse, built from 1756 to 1759, the engineer John Smeaton investigated which limes set under water, work that led toward Portland cement, patented by Joseph Aspdin in 1824. What remains debated is how routine hot mixing was across the Roman world.

title: Damascus Steel
description: Indian crucible steel, the trace impurity behind its pattern, and the nanotube headlines

concepts.title: Watered Steel
concepts.contentHtml:
For centuries Europeans prized swords from the Middle East whose blades showed a flowing pattern, like running water, wood grain or a ladder, that lay in the metal itself rather than being etched on top. These became known as Damascus blades. The name most likely comes from the city, a great trading center where imported steel was forged into swords, though there is no evidence that the steel itself was made there; another theory links it to an Arabic word for the watered pattern. The 9th-century philosopher al-Kindi already wrote of Damascene swords in a treatise on blades.

The steel came mostly from much farther east. Smiths in South India and Sri Lanka sealed iron and carbon-rich plant matter in clay crucibles and heated them for hours in a furnace, producing small cakes of steel. Crucible steelmaking there goes back to around the middle of the 1st millennium BCE, and ingots were traded west for centuries to be forged in Persia and Syria. The steel is now called wootz, an English rendering of South Indian words for steel, such as Kannada and Telugu ukku. It is ultrahigh-carbon steel, roughly 1 to 2 percent carbon, far more than ordinary blade steel.

Europe studied it late. Samples reached Joseph Banks in London in 1790, and George Pearson published the first chemical analysis in 1795. Legends grew alongside: blades that could slice a silk scarf floating in the air, and a grim story that smiths quenched blades in the bodies of enslaved people. The second traces to an 1894 newspaper hoax in the Chicago Tribune that quoted a fictional professor.

concepts.title: Why the Pattern Vanished
concepts.contentHtml:
The pattern comes from structure inside the steel. In slowly cooled wootz, some carbon forms hard particles of iron carbide, called cementite. Forging at fairly low temperatures, over many heating cycles, lined these particles up into bands within a softer steel. Etching with acid then showed the bands as light and dark swirls. Too much heat dissolves the carbides and erases the pattern, so the smith's skill mattered as much as the ingot.

Why the pattern sometimes formed and sometimes did not was worked out by John Verhoeven, a metallurgist at Iowa State University, and Alfred Pendray, a bladesmith, working through the 1990s. In a 1998 paper, "The key role of impurities in ancient Damascus steel blades," they reported the decisive factor: tiny traces of carbide-forming elements, especially vanadium. These segregate into thin zones as the steel solidifies, and during the forging cycles carbides cluster along them. They argued that the classic blades depended on ore from particular Indian sources that happened to carry such traces.

Smiths had no way to know the key lay in a trace element, so a change of ore could ruin results without anyone understanding why. Even Michael Faraday analyzed wootz and wrongly suspected aluminum was the key. Other pressures added up: disrupted trade, the sword's declining role in war, and colonial-era taxes and restrictions on Indian ironmaking. Production dwindled to almost nothing by about 1900; Ananda Coomaraswamy's 1903 account of crucible steelmaking in Sri Lanka is the last recorded. In 1841 Pavel Anosov of the Zlatoust arms works in the Urals published a treatise claiming to have recovered the secret of patterned bulat steel.

concepts.title: Nanotubes, Hype and Reproductions
concepts.contentHtml:
In November 2006 a team at the Technical University of Dresden, including Peter Paufler, reported in Nature that a sample from a 17th-century Damascus sabre contained carbon nanotubes and nanowires of cementite, seen with high-resolution transmission electron microscopy. The paper, "Carbon nanotubes in an ancient Damascus sabre," suggested the nanostructure might help explain the blade's banding. Headlines followed: medieval smiths as nanotechnologists.

Caution is warranted. Identifying nanotubes inside heavily worked steel is difficult; Verhoeven suggested the features could be cementite structures rather than tubes, and later studies have not confirmed the finding. Even if nanotubes are present, they would be a by-product of forging, not something the smiths knew about or aimed for, and they are far smaller than the bands of the pattern, which are visible to the naked eye. The fair summary is that the claim is unconfirmed.

The "lost forever" story is overstated too. Verhoeven and Pendray produced blades whose internal structure and surface pattern match museum originals, using crucible steel with small additions of vanadium and repeated forging cycles. What remains unknown is the exact practice of particular historical workshops and whether smiths chose ores deliberately. Note also that most modern knives sold as "Damascus" are pattern-welded: layers of different steels forged together and etched. The bladesmith William Moran popularized that technique under the Damascus name from 1973. Pattern welding has its own long history in early medieval Europe, but it is not wootz.

title: Silphium
description: The plant on Cyrene's coins, its uses, and the last stalk sent to Nero

concepts.title: The Plant on the Coins
concepts.contentHtml:
Silver coins of Cyrene, a Greek city in what is now eastern Libya, show a plant with a thick stalk, paired leaves and a rounded flower head. It was silphium, and it paid for the city. Cyrene was founded around 631 BCE by settlers from the island of Thera, and silphium, which grew wild in the land around it, became its great export. The Roman poet Catullus could describe the region simply as "silphium-bearing Cyrene."

A Spartan drinking cup of about 565 to 560 BCE, now in Paris and known as the Arcesilas cup, shows King Arcesilas II of Cyrene watching workers weigh and store bales of some commodity. It was long identified as silphium, though many scholars now favor wool. Whatever the cargo, the plant was valuable for centuries. Pliny the Elder records that Julius Caesar, at the start of the civil war in 49 BCE, took 1,500 Roman pounds of silphium from the state treasury along with its gold and silver.

The plant could not be farmed. Theophrastus, Aristotle's successor, wrote in the late 4th century BCE that silphium grew only wild and resisted cultivation, and he noted that his sources disagreed about what it looked like. The prized product was the resin, Latin laser or laserpicium, drawn from the root and stalk. Herodotus placed its range in a strip of coastal Libya.

concepts.title: Seasoning, Medicine and a Contested Contraceptive
concepts.contentHtml:
Greeks and Romans used silphium in the kitchen: the stalks were eaten and the resin flavored sauces, and the Roman recipe collection attributed to Apicius calls for laser in many dishes. Physicians prescribed it for coughs, fevers, sore throats, warts and much else. Its reputation outlived the plant; medical writers kept listing it long after genuine Cyrenaic silphium had become scarce, which makes it hard to know what later patients actually received.

The most debated use is as a contraceptive. The 2nd-century CE physician Soranus of Ephesus, in his work on gynecology, includes "Cyrenaic juice" among drugs taken to prevent conception. The historian John Riddle argued in Contraception and Abortion from the Ancient World to the Renaissance (1992) that several ancient plant contraceptives, silphium among them, may have had real effects, and that ancient women had more control over fertility than historians had assumed. Other scholars doubt that such drugs were reliable or that ancient reports can be checked. Since the plant cannot be identified, the question cannot be tested directly.

A popular modern claim links silphium to the heart symbol, because the seed or fruit shown on some Cyrenean coins is heart-shaped. The resemblance is real. A connection to the later Valentine heart is speculation, with no documentary chain behind it, and the heart symbol has other proposed origins.

concepts.title: The Last Stalk
concepts.contentHtml:
Pliny the Elder, writing in the 70s CE, reported that silphium had not been found in Cyrenaica for many years. He blamed the tax farmers who leased the pastures, who found it more profitable to let flocks graze the land bare. Within living memory, he wrote, only a single stalk had been found there, and it was sent to the emperor Nero, who reigned from 54 to 68 CE, as a curiosity. Silphium is therefore often called the first recorded extinction, though that label assumes we know what the plant was.

Explanations have multiplied. Overgrazing and overharvesting are the classic ones. In 2022 Paul Pollaro and Paul Robertson argued that human-caused environmental change in ancient Cyrenaica, as deforestation and farming led to desertification, was the main driver, squeezing a plant confined to a narrow band of habitat. Others have suggested that silphium was a largely sterile hybrid that spread mainly by its roots, which would also explain why it could not be grown from seed. All of these are hypotheses resting on thin evidence.

Rome adapted. Pliny says that for a long time the only laser imported came from Persia, Media and Armenia and was inferior; that substitute was probably asafoetida, the pungent resin of Ferula assa-foetida still used in Indian cooking. The Apicius collection even gives a trick for stretching an ounce of laser: keep it in a jar with pine nuts and cook with the nuts. Whether silphium survives anywhere is open. Since 2021 the Turkish pharmacognosist Mahmut Miski has argued that Ferula drudeana, a rare plant endemic to Turkey, matches ancient descriptions. The case is suggestive but unproven, not least because the plant grows far from Libya.

title: Family Secrets and Workshop Recipes
description: The Chamberlen forceps, the color-changing Lycurgus Cup, and the glassmakers of Murano

concepts.title: Forceps in a Locked Box
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1813 a hidden cache turned up in the attic of Woodham Mortimer Hall, a house near Maldon in Essex: old coins, gloves, trinkets and a set of midwifery instruments, including obstetric forceps. The house had belonged to the physician Peter Chamberlen, and the find confirmed a family story more than two centuries old.

The Chamberlens were Huguenots who left France for England in 1569 to escape religious violence. Peter Chamberlen the elder (c. 1560 to 1631), a barber-surgeon and man-midwife who attended the queens of James I and Charles I, probably devised the forceps around 1600: two curved blades, inserted one at a time and then locked together, that could guide a baby's head out in an obstructed labor. Before then a surgeon facing such a birth often had to sacrifice the child to save the mother. The family kept the device secret. It was carried into the birthing room in a lined box, everyone else was sent out, and the mother was blindfolded.

In 1670 Hugh Chamberlen, the elder Peter's grandnephew, tried to sell the secret in Paris to François Mauriceau, the leading French obstetrician. Mauriceau tested him on a woman he judged impossible to deliver because of a badly deformed pelvis. Hugh failed after hours of effort, and mother and child died. In 1672 Hugh published an English translation of Mauriceau's textbook, with a preface alluding to his family's method. He later appears to have sold the secret to Dutch practitioners, though what they received is doubtful. By the 1720s and 1730s versions of the forceps were public. The family had kept its secret for over a century; the figure usually quoted is about 150 years.

concepts.title: The Cup That Changes Color
concepts.contentHtml:
The British Museum holds a Roman glass cup about 16 centimeters tall, made in the 4th century CE. In light reflected from its surface it looks jade green; lit from behind or within, it glows ruby red. Its carved scene shows the myth of King Lycurgus, who attacked Ambrosia, a follower of Dionysus; she turned into a vine and trapped him. The Lycurgus Cup is a cage cup, or diatretum: the figures were cut from a thick glass blank until they stand almost free of the wall.

In 1990 David Barber and Ian Freestone examined fragments with an analytical transmission electron microscope. The glass contains tiny amounts of silver and gold, roughly 300 parts per million of silver and 40 of gold, present as alloy particles around 70 nanometers across. Particles that small interact with light through surface plasmons, collective oscillations of the metal's electrons. They absorb and scatter particular wavelengths: light scattered back toward a viewer looks green, while light passing through has lost much of its green and looks red.

The Romans could not have known about nanoparticles, and very few dichroic Roman glass fragments survive, with colors that vary widely, which suggests the effect was hard to control. Some researchers think the glass was deliberately dosed with gold and silver in some form; others suspect accidental contamination. Either way, what was lost was a workshop recipe. In the 17th century Johann Kunckel at Potsdam and others made gold ruby glass on purpose, Michael Faraday studied the colors of colloidal gold in 1857, and the glassmaker Corning has reproduced a glass blank of similar composition and structure.

concepts.title: Venice and the Leaky Secret
concepts.contentHtml:
On 8 November 1291 the government of Venice ordered most of the city's glass furnaces moved to the island of Murano. The stated reason was fire: furnaces among wooden houses were dangerous. The move also concentrated the craft, its workers and its know-how where the state could watch them. Glassmakers received privileges; from 1376 a glassmaker's daughter who married a nobleman kept her rank, and her children were nobles. They also faced restrictions. They could not leave without permission, and often-repeated accounts say that deserters' families could be jailed and agents sent after those who refused to return.

The secrets were worth guarding. In the 1450s Angelo Barovier is credited with cristallo, a soda glass clear enough to resemble rock crystal, made with manganese among its ingredients. Murano glass dominated Europe's luxury market.

The walls leaked anyway. Rival rulers tempted workers away, and by the late 16th century glass in the Venetian style, façon de Venise, was made across Europe, usually of lower quality. In 1612 the Florentine priest Antonio Neri printed L'Arte Vetraria, a manual of glass recipes that carried Venetian methods into print. In 1665 Jean-Baptiste Colbert, Louis XIV's minister, founded the Royal Mirror-Glass Factory, ancestor of today's Saint-Gobain, employing Venetian glassworkers enticed to Paris, and in 1678 it began supplying glass for the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.

title: Why Know-How Vanishes
description: A modern lost material, the mechanisms of loss, and the overstated claim that we cannot replicate the past

concepts.title: Fogbank: Lost in the Nuclear Age
concepts.contentHtml:
Around 2000 the US National Nuclear Security Administration began a life-extension program for the W76, a warhead carried on submarine-launched missiles, and found it could no longer make one of the parts. The material, code-named Fogbank, had been produced at a facility in the Y-12 complex at Oak Ridge, Tennessee, from 1975 to 1989. The building had since been shut, few records of the process had been kept, and most of the people who knew it had left. What Fogbank is remains classified; outside experts believe it is an aerogel-like material used between the stages of the weapon.

The agency chose to remake it rather than find a substitute, and engineers failed repeatedly. It spent about $23 million on an alternative and then $69 million more to manufacture Fogbank, and deliveries of refurbished warheads ran late. The root-cause investigation found something no one had written down: the original purification step left an impurity that subtly changed the material, and a later step depended on it. Newer purification removed more of the impurity and spoiled the product. The fix was to add the impurity back deliberately and monitor it.

The parallel with Damascus steel is close. In both cases a property depended on a trace substance the makers did not know was essential, so changing the source or the equipment broke the process silently. Lost technology is not only an ancient problem: any skill held by a few people, at a single plant or in an undocumented quirk of a process, can disappear within one working lifetime. Fogbank was lost about a decade after its plant closed.

concepts.title: How Knowledge Gets Lost
concepts.contentHtml:
The cases in this topic suggest a short list of mechanisms. The first is secrecy: Greek fire and the Chamberlen forceps were deliberately confined to a few people, so the knowledge faded or died with them. The second is tacit skill. The chemist and philosopher Michael Polanyi wrote in The Tacit Dimension (1966) that "we can know more than we can tell." Forging a wootz blade or fitting an Inca wall depended on judgment in the hands, learned by apprenticeship. In a 1974 study the sociologist Harry Collins found that laboratories trying to build a new kind of laser, the TEA laser, succeeded only when they had personal contact with someone who had already built one; published papers were not enough.

The third is single sources. Silphium grew in one region and resisted farming; Damascus patterns probably depended on particular Indian ores; Byzantine fire probably needed oil from the Black Sea region; Roman harbor builders shipped ash from the Bay of Naples. The fourth is collapse of demand and organization: when the western Roman building economy broke down, the workforce and supply chains for huge concrete vaults went with it.

The fifth is fragile records. A single shipwreck preserved the Antikythera mechanism, covered in another topic, and nothing of comparable gearing survives from the next thousand years and more. Cicero mentions a planetary sphere attributed to Archimedes, brought to Rome after Syracuse fell in 212 BCE, but no account of how such devices were built survives. Usually several mechanisms act together, and the evidence of what was lost is itself thin: often a few lines in a chronicle are all that show something existed.

concepts.title: The Replication Myth: Inca Walls
concepts.contentHtml:
Inca walls at Cusco, Sacsayhuamán and Ollantaytambo fit blocks of hard stone so tightly, without mortar, that a knife blade cannot enter the joints. They are a favorite of claims that ancient builders used techniques modern people cannot reproduce, and Andean folklore said the masons could soften rock with a plant. Earthquakes, including one in 1650, wrecked the Dominican buildings raised over the Qorikancha temple in Cusco, while the Inca walls beneath still stand.

In the early 1980s the Swiss-born architect Jean-Pierre Protzen of the University of California, Berkeley, went to Inca quarries, Kachiqhata near Ollantaytambo and Rumiqolqa near Cusco, and tried the work himself. Using river cobbles as hammerstones, he found he could dress faces and edges of the building stone by pounding. He argued that blocks were fitted by trial and error: setting a stone against its neighbor, seeing where they touched, pounding those spots down and trying again. Hammer marks visible on the faces of many Inca stones fit that picture. He published in Scientific American in 1986 and in a book on Ollantaytambo in 1993.

Across this topic the same pattern holds. Researchers have reproduced a working Byzantine-style petroleum flamethrower, self-healing hot-mixed concrete, patterned crucible steel and color-changing gold and silver glass. What remains genuinely unknown is narrower: the exact Byzantine recipe and siphon design, the identity of silphium, the routines of particular workshops, and many details of how the Inca moved their largest stones.
